Chapter 4: Faith, Doubt, and the Power of Revelation
In Mormonism, there’s this deeply held belief that God is still speaking to his people. For a lot of folks, that’s a huge comfort—it makes faith feel alive, like the divine is woven right into ordinary life.
But here’s the thing—that same belief can also spark conflict and confusion. What happens when someone trusts their own visions more than the wisdom of their community? You can probably imagine how tricky that gets.
Just look at the Lafferty brothers. Their path into extremism really took off when they started relying almost entirely on personal revelation. Stepping away from the mainstream church, they began searching for answers straight from God, convinced that every prayer, every dream, was a message meant just for them.
Over time, those so-called revelations got more urgent, even more demanding. The brothers became convinced they’d been chosen for something special—a mission so important, it led them to consider breaking the very laws they once held sacred.
For most of us, faith is supposed to be a source of strength—a way to feel connected, to make sense of the chaos around us. But here’s something to pay attention to: when faith drifts away from reason, when it loses that grounding, it can pull people toward really dark places.
The Lafferty brothers’ story is a powerful reminder of how easily devotion can blur into delusion.
As the days led up to the crime, the brothers became more and more cut off from the world. Hours spent in prayer, always searching for signs or omens. Every setback? They saw it as a test from God. Whenever someone pushed back—whether it was family, church leaders, or anyone else—they took it as proof they were on the right track.
That’s the thing about revelation—it feels so intimate, so personal. If you believe God’s talking right to you, who could possibly convince you otherwise? Doubt starts to seem like a weakness, something you have to fight off. For the Lafferty brothers, their certainty became a kind of armor, shielding them from any worries or second thoughts that might’ve stopped them.
But real faith isn’t just about being certain all the time. At its best, it comes with humility—a willingness to admit you might be wrong, to listen to others, even when it’s hard. In fundamentalist Mormonism, though, that humility can be tough to find. When everyone’s encouraged to seek their own revelations, it’s easy for each person to feel like their own prophet, accountable only to God.
The tragedy that unfolded in that Utah town wasn’t just about two men and their choices. It was also about a culture—one that, for all its strengths, sometimes overlooks the dangers of belief when it runs wild and unchecked.
The Lafferty brothers’ story stands as a warning: when faith loses its balance with reason and compassion, it can turn into something destructive.
